Over the course of an evening, the characters’ continual wink-and-nudge reminders of the goofiness of their world make it harder to maintain investment.
And yet “The Cottage” doesn’t sustain the kind of adrenaline needed to keep non-farce-lovers from lapsing into lethargy.
Tellingly, that physical prop gag is funnier than any one line of dialogue in this entire witless play.
The forbidden-fruit pleasures that “The Cottage” tries to pass off as a feast, in a lavish production directed by Jason Alexander, are familiar, superficial and fleeting.
Audience members seemed eager to yield to Rustin’s shticks and howl along, but in reality there’s more delight in looking at ‘The Cottage’ than laughing along to it.
Alexander’s trick-filled production, which opened on Monday at the Theater, cannot hide that the stakes are too low.
The Cottage is a fresh and fiercely fun play that's firing on all cylinders, with Rustin's excellent script.

The Cottage more than fits that bill. It’s no real surprise that it works as well as it does. Director Jason Alexander (Seinfeld) knows how to do smart yet silly comedy without overdoing it, and The Cottage is a play that needs only light touches to make it frothy and effervescent.
This is Jason Alexander‘s Broadway directorial debut and he shines in bringing all the varied pieces together to present a playdate of delight for everyone.

But long before the curtain call, not even the terrifically appealing cast nor the much-welcome air conditioning could dissuade me from seeing this ersatz 1920s British comedy of manners as a tedious two-hour exercise in comic overkill.

Although Sandy Rustin’s The Cottage, now arrived at Broadway’s Theater, bills itself as “A Romantic and (Not Quite) Murderous Comedy of Manners,” it is devoid of the two requirements of drawing room comedy: wit and quotable one-liners.
It's a tasteless, anything-goes enterprise that, ruthlessly milking its often-coarse comic bits, gives artifice a bad name.

Sitting through this forced, unfunny take on British sex comedies of yore, I was reminded of an equally inept exercise in pandering to the tourist trade before that particular play was also run out of town.
This is a production that succeeds in its mission, solely to entertain and treat the audience to some lighthearted laughter.
“The Cottage” would have worked better as simply an outright farcical comedy with no attempt at seriousness.

Jason Alexander, who played the famously neurotic George Costanza on Seinfeld for nine seasons, directs a seasoned cast that climbs an uphill battle to excavate witty banter from a predictable plot that rarely stays ahead of the audience.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Noël Coward-inspired farce, with some finding it a delightful, breezy summer romp while others dismiss it as hackneyed and unfunny, lacking the wit and sophistication of the classics it emulates.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.

vr.q: if you're looking for a good comedy play I would definitely recommend The Cottage. I think it's really funny, the cast is incredible, the set is incredible, and I think you'll have a good time!
When it's good, it's really, really good and really, really funny... ultimately, the end, for me just didn't pack the punch that I wanted it to considering how funny the first act is.
The story itself is nothing groundbreaking, but the performances sell it, and the use of physicality is really fun too.
